p14.text: Paper diorama: the Primepaw shell built as cardboard and paper cut-outs laid on one cream sheet, lit from the top left so each piece casts one shadow down and to the right. The rail, the sessions board, the capsule mats and the composer frame are cardboard: thick, with a darker cut edge along the bottom and the right. The chat column is a sheet of paper level with the sessions board, with the thread and the composer on a second sheet laid over the tabs. Sessions are paper strips, the workspace headers sage strips, the capsules cream plates on green mats with the time badge straddling the edge. The rail icons and the paw are solid-colour die-cut stickers, the active one ringed in gold; badges, dots, the pinwheel, the busy pill and the cat peeking over the composer are stickers too. The composer has a mic disc beside the send disc: pressed, it latches flat and turns red, the hint gives way to a sound trace in red pen and the time by hand, and what you say lands in the box word by word; press it again or Esc to stop. Stickers are stuck flat, so they have a white cut border and no shadow. Boards run edge to edge with a 3px margin. The Advanced options switch is a thick-card pull-tab sliding in a slot cut into the paper, with on and off handwritten in the slot, YOLO is a rubber stamp, a faded black outline when off and red ink when on, and the effort levels and the picker checks follow the Kraft toggles: cardboard that stays pressed flat when on, terracotta for Max, a green sticker check on a picked row. The white paper (the chat sheet, the leaf, the rows and fields) carries the paper texture of the Factory Overseer workshop walls with its colour kept; cardboard is a flecked board; the workspace headers are paper strips in their workspace’s colour with the rows’ texture, their count and caret written in pen ink, and the first session tucks under its header; an open session’s title bar and tab strip take the same paper colour as its workspace header, with unselected tabs a lighter cut of it; the prompt box stays plain. The rail icons, the Select button and every other button are cut-outs in their own colours carrying the same paper texture as the chat sheet and the session rows, not stickers. Sessions under a header stack like a deck of cards, hovering one shows a three-dot menu mark at its far right, and a working session carries a paper pinwheel: four coloured blades with folded tips on an ink pin, turning. Same live demo, same Night toggle.

p15.text: Dark mode: the same diorama after dark, opening in the night theme (the rail button flips it back to day). Boards go dark brown, paper warm charcoal, and every texture switches to its night tile. Identity colours on buttons are mixed down into the desk so white glyphs stay readable.

p16.text: The other screens, light on the left and dark on the right. Each is a live demo on the same materials: a cardboard rail with coloured thick-card tiles, one paper sheet for the content, paper pieces with the wall texture, thick-card buttons, sticker pills and rubber stamps inked on the paper.

p17.text: A session with its side panel open. Two tabs at the right of the strip open it. Artifacts are clipped to a cardboard clipboard: one tab per artifact, a version stepper, and Copy, Download and Ask on the side under the sheet. Each artifact also shows in the thread as a paper chip with a folded corner, which turns highlighter yellow while it is the one on the clipboard. A web page artifact is a white printout taped to the sheet, because it has its own design. The side chat is a legal pad: asides stay out of the session, the session keeps working meanwhile, and Put in chat carries an answer into the composer. With both open they stack, so you can read and ask at once. The left edge of the panel drags to resize. All the contents are fake.

p18.text: When the agent needs you, the turn stops and something on an amber mat waits for you. It holds still: the amber, the Needs you sticker and the badge on the session row are the signal. A tool approval is a permission slip in the thread with the command or diff, what it will do, and Allow once, Allow for this session or Deny. Questions wait in the dock above the composer as one card: the session agent’s portrait, implementer-agent has 3 questions, and Answer. Answer opens a sheet with a folder tab per question, labelled from the question with a tick once it has an answer. Each tab gives the problem in a few plain sentences, the question on one line, then the options: buttons, or checkboxes when you can pick more than one, each with a line of context under it and at most one Recommended sticker. Submit sends them all at once and says how many are left until then. The inbox shows the same card and sheet. Either way you can just write in the composer instead. Your choice is struck with a rubber stamp, the thread keeps a stub of it, and the agent carries on. YOLO now belongs to the session, skips slips but not questions, and turning it on approves a waiting slip. Try it: these two boards are one flow in ORB-272, and with YOLO off any message you send stops at an edit slip.

p19.text: Knowledge base: the book on the rail. The notes board is a file tree on one sheet of paper: nested folders and .md files with their git state. The note is a sheet of paper: type, title, description and tags on top, then blocks you can drag by the grip to move. Drag a list bullet to move an item, or drop it onto another item to nest it. Parent, related, links and backlinks sit in the margin. Graph is react-force-graph on cork: index cards strung with thread that you drag, zoom and click open. The second pair starts on setting up: pick a folder or clone a repo.

p20.text: Home, the page at /: you talk to one personal agent, Jarvis, and it starts the sessions. Jarvis tops the rail as a cream tile with its portrait, a cat in a bow tie, badged with the threads waiting on you. Threads are paper strips, newest first, with the last thing said, the time and a badge when something waits on you; rename and archive are in each row’s menu. In a thread your words are kraft notes and Jarvis’s are set in Fraunces. Jarvis leaves three kinds of cards: a session card for every session it starts, with the workspace strip in the workspace’s colour, branch, model, a live status sticker and the session’s last line; a helper card, an index card folded to one line, for a read-only look into the code; and a decision line for every call Thread YOLO makes. A job ends on a finish report on the sage mat. The header has the title, how many sessions the thread started, and the Thread YOLO stamp, off by default, which says what it risks when you strike it. Everything is fake.

p21.text: The states: empty, a big prompt box where sending starts a thread; a session waiting on you, on the amber mat, next to one that failed; Jarvis asking which workspace with the same question card and sheet a session uses; and Thread YOLO on, which answers waiting prompts and writes each call down. Turn YOLO on in Bump Node to 22 to watch it answer the waiting session.

p23.text: Home before there is a main agent: the same form, as a card in the middle of the empty sheet, with the rail’s top tile an empty taped frame and the thread column waiting. Press Create with nothing typed and the rule under the name turns dashed red with “It needs a name” under it in red pen; with a name, the WELCOME stamp lands, the portrait drops onto the rail tile, and the sheet turns into the empty home page where the agent says hello in its own words. The second pair is that moment.

p24.text: Inbox: everything that needs you, on the tray tile right after Jarvis’s with the unread count as its sticker. The left board is conversations, one paper strip per request: a thread with Jarvis, else a factory task, else a session, with the source on a small chip, the newest line, the time, a blue dot while something is unread and a red sticker counting what needs an answer. Five small cards filter it: Needs answer, Reports, PRs, Factory, All. The sheet is the chosen conversation’s items in time order. A question sits on the amber mat with prompt 1’s options and is answered in place; under it, Ask about this is a short thread that stays attached to the question, your note on kraft and Jarvis’s answer in serif. An approval is the same slip as in the session. A finish report sits on the sage mat. A pull request that needs your review is a card on the amber mat with the PR chip, the branch, its size and checks, and the first line of its description; Approve stamps it here, Open the PR goes to GitHub. A factory task is a card with its state as a sticker: Blocked in red with the reason, Waiting on you, or Ready for you in Planning with a button to the Plan tab. Answered items fold to a stub and say who answered by hand: You, Jarvis (Thread YOLO), or You, through Jarvis. Each item has a read mark and Done, which files it with an Undo. The second pair has nothing left in it. On the third, the push in Add CSV export gets allowed by Jarvis under Thread YOLO while you look: the stamp lands, the slip folds, the sticker and the rail count drop.

p25.text: Factory: every factory at a glance, on the factory tile after Kanban’s. One card per factory on the sheet: its name by hand, its board as a dashed link (primepaw issues →), a state sticker (Running green, Idle a plain paper label, Off a dashed ghost, Paused amber under the global pause) and the factory’s own switch. Under them five counts by hand with their words: in flight, waiting on you, Blocked, to plan, queued; zeros go faint, waiting on you is amber, Blocked red, and a card with either sits on the amber mat. Along the bottom the steps that are on, as small chips joined by arrows: Planning → Plan review → Implementation → Testing → Code review → Merge; a step that is off is a dashed ghost with only its icon. The header has New factory, which opens a short menu of the boards that have none, and Factory settings. Above the cards, Pause all factories is the slot switch with its consequence in one line by hand: nothing new starts, what is in flight finishes its step and waits. Nothing pulses. The second pair has no factories yet, and New factory is the way in. On the third every factory is paused. On the fourth PrimePaw has a Blocked task, with the reason in red and the way to it.

p26.text: Jarvis, the main agent’s character: Button, a round cat in a bow tie, cut from cream and kraft in 1.6px ink, picked from five cuts. This sheet lays out every piece he is cut into. The cut: the kraft patch over his right ear, bead eyes, blush, a red nose, the red bow, two paws to hold an edge, with the paper’s cut edge around him (a light rim by day, white at night). The portrait: the same face as a flat sticker with a white die-cut rim and no shadow, never pixel art, on the cream tile that tops every rail, as the first Meet your Main Agent photo, and at the head of the threads board. Over the composer he is 92px wide, in from the right, leaning 4 degrees on his paws; over the empty home’s greeting he is 84px. He is a cut-out, not an animation: he never blinks, bounces, pulses, changes face with a session’s state, or does anything when clicked. The drawing is Kraft’s Characters asset, jarvis.svg.

p22.text: Setting up: the checklist a new install opens on, six steps on one sheet with a tick box each, the open one unfolded. Meet your Main Agent is the only step that has to be done before Open Primepaw works. It is a form on the paper: the name on a ruled line with Jarvis pencilled in as the placeholder, six portrait stickers taped on like photos with the picked one ringed in pen, and the model, which is the global default until the pull-tab says otherwise and then a provider and a model from torn-paper pickers. One line says what the agent is for: it starts work for you and never edits code itself. Create with no name writes “It needs a name” in red pen; with one, a WELCOME stamp lands and the step folds to done. The second pair restored a backup, so the step is already ticked: Jarvis came with your backup. Choose a backup on the first pair does the same.
